newsitem.title: USA: U.S. senators press Glickman to act on dairy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. senators press Glickman to act on dairy.

text.p: U.S. senators Thursday pressed Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman to set a national cheese price or take other action to help milk producers reeling from lower prices and higher production costs.
"There is a real crisis in the milk industry today with prices being so very low," said Sen. Arlen Specter, Pennsylvania Republican, who requested the hearing by a Senate Appropriations subcommittee.
"There is a feeling of tremendous urgency, that's why I think the secretary should act swiftly..." added Sen. Russell Feingold, Democrat from Wisconsin, another major dairy state.

USDA currently uses the National Cheese Exchange (NCE) in Greenbay, Wisc., as part of its calculations of dairy prices. But critics say because a small amount of cheese is traded on the exchange it is not a fair representation of prices. Some blamed the NCE for a sharp drop in milk prices late last year.

The department is getting public comment on whether to delink the exchange as a factor in its dairy formula price. In addition, Glickman told the Senate panel USDA this week began a voluntary national survey of cheddar cheese prices.

Specter grilled the secretary and other top USDA officials on how long it would take to finetune the survey so that it could replace the NCE as a price gauge and said he would propose legislation to require producers to provide information if the voluntary survey proved lacking.
The lawmaker balked at USDA estimates of six to eight weeks to cement the survey and demanded a list of the 112 plants to be polled weekly so his staff could begin calling themselves.
Glickman defended the department, saying the cheese price was only one part of the puzzle.

"This cheese price is a problem. But it is not the main problem. The problems go to a much bigger picture and they frankly go to the fact that for years and years and years the government supported dairy products at high support levels and now it's ended," Glickman said.
"And now we're going through this free market gyration with high volatility and highly variable prices," he said.

Glickman said he wanted to move as fast as possible on the cheese price but said he believed the "big difference" for milk producers would come with the reform of federal milk marketing orders as required by the 1996 Farm Bill.
